newsitem.title: USA: U.S. court voids order to Swiss banks on Marcos funds.
newsitem.headline: U.S. court voids order to Swiss banks on Marcos funds.

text.p: A U.S. Appeals Court on Wednesday annuled a lower court's order that two Swiss banks must turn over an estimated $475 million from accounts linked to late Philippine dictator Ferdinand Marcos.

The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, in a written ruling released in San Francisco, said U.S. District Judge Manuel Real of Los Angeles had no authority to order the banks to turn over the contested funds to court custody.
Swiss Bank Corp and Credit Suisse, two major Swiss banks, had appealed Real's order, made in December last year.

Real's order had also drawn protests from the Swiss government, which had warned the United States that any effort by U.S. courts to enforce the order by imposing sanctions on the banks would conflict with international and Swiss law, according to published reports.
Under Real's order, the money would have been turned over to the U.S. court so that rival claims could be decided.
But the appeals court overturned his order, saying he "had no authority to order the banks to deposit the contested funds into the court registry."
The court case stems from attempts by victims of the Marcos government to secure payment of a huge court judgement they won against the Marcos estate.
In 1994, a federal jury in a class action civil rights suit in Hawaii awarded $1.9 billion to 9,500 victims and family members of victims who suffered at the hands of Marcos's government.

The Honolulu jury found that Marcos, who died there in exile in 1989, was responsible for major human rights abuses, including torture, murder and the "disappearances" of Filipinos during his rule that ended in 1986.

Representatives of the victims served "notices of levy" on the Los Angeles branches of Credit Suisse and Swiss Bank Corp last year in an attempt to recover hundreds of millions of dollars linked to Marcos that they allege are held by the two Swiss banks.
But the banks said that the Los Angeles offices had no deposit accounts linked to Marcos and no access to information concerning the banks' deposit accounts in Switzerland.

The appeals court said California law required creditors to personally serve an officer of the bank branch at which a deposit account was held. The Marcos accounts were not held at the banks' Los Angeles offices and the notices were therefore ineffective, it said in its ruling.
The Swiss banks have never publicly stated how much money is in the Marcos-linked deposits, but they are estimated to contain some $475 million.

The Marcos accounts in Switzerland were frozen by Swiss authorities in 1986 at the request of the Philippines government. The Philippines government has also claimed the Swiss funds, alleging they were stolen from government coffers.

The Swiss banks have voiced concern about having to pay out twice in case of conflicting court rulings. Negotiations have been held among the various parties to try to resolve the dispute over the competing claims but have so far failed to find a solution.
